title: Strength Training Cuts Type 2 Diabetes Risk by Up to 62% — and Consistency Matters More Than Intensity
excerpt: A study of nearly 144,000 people over 19 years found that regular weight training — especially when combined with cardio and less screen time — offers powerful diabetes protection that South Asians have extra reason to pay attention to.
body:
If you've ever wondered whether those dumbbells gathering dust in the corner could do more than build visible muscle, a new study has a definitive answer — and it's especially relevant if you're South Asian.

Research published in JAMA Network Open, drawing on data from 143,715 U.S. healthcare professionals tracked over nearly 19 years, has found that consistent strength training can reduce the risk of developing type 2 diabetes by up to 62 percent. The caveat: it's not just about picking up weights occasionally. The study makes clear that how long you stick with it matters far more than how hard you go on any single day.

## The Numbers That Matter

Compared with people who did no resistance training at all, those who logged at least two hours of strength training per week had a **27 percent lower risk** of type 2 diabetes. That alone is striking, but the data gets more compelling when you zoom in on sustained habits.

Adults who consistently performed at least 30 minutes of strength training weekly between the ages of 40 and 60 had a **42 percent lower risk** compared with those who rarely trained. People who gradually increased their training over time also saw meaningful benefits. Those with inconsistent, stop-and-start patterns? Essentially no protection.

The strongest finding came from participants who combined all three behaviors: at least one hour of weekly strength training, recommended levels of aerobic exercise, and less than two hours of daily television. Their diabetes risk dropped by a remarkable **62 percent**.



> **"A landmark study in *The Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology* has shown that metabolic dysfunction often begins in South Asians at a BMI that would be classified as "normal" by Western standards."**


## Why This Matters for South Asians

Type 2 diabetes is sometimes called a "South Asian epidemic" — and the data backs up the concern. Indians and people of South Asian descent develop insulin resistance and diabetes at significantly lower body weights and younger ages than many other populations. A landmark study in *The Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology* has shown that metabolic dysfunction often begins in South Asians at a BMI that would be classified as "normal" by Western standards.

For the Indian diaspora — particularly NRIs in the US, UK, and Canada living increasingly sedentary lives in desk-bound tech jobs — the implications are pointed. The typical South Asian lifestyle in Western countries often involves long work hours, minimal structured exercise, and food environments that combine traditional high-carbohydrate diets with Western ultra-processed additions.

Strength training specifically addresses this vulnerability. Unlike aerobic exercise alone, resistance training builds lean muscle mass, which acts as a glucose sink — helping the body absorb blood sugar more efficiently. This mechanism is particularly valuable for people with the "thin-fat" phenotype common among South Asians, where relatively low overall body weight masks disproportionately high visceral fat and poor muscle-to-fat ratios.

## What "Consistent" Actually Means

The study's authors note that the key variable wasn't the type of exercise or the weight being lifted — it was the pattern of sustained engagement over years. Researchers tracked participants through repeated assessments, measuring whether their exercise habits stayed stable, increased, decreased, or fluctuated.

Those who started strength training in middle age and maintained it — even at moderate levels — accumulated protection over time. The researchers describe it as a dose-response relationship: more consistency yielded greater risk reduction, without requiring extreme intensity.

For practical purposes, the study suggests that two to three sessions per week of moderate resistance training — bodyweight exercises, dumbbells, resistance bands, or gym machines — combined with regular walking or cycling and reduced sedentary screen time, represents an achievable formula with outsized returns.

## The Bigger Picture

More than 100 million Indians now live with type 2 diabetes, and the International Diabetes Federation projects that number will exceed 150 million by 2045. Among the diaspora, rates are climbing too — Indian Americans have diabetes prevalence rates roughly double that of non-Hispanic white Americans.

This study adds weight to a growing body of evidence that prevention doesn't require dramatic lifestyle overhauls. It requires, above all, **showing up consistently** — two to three times a week, year after year. For a community with elevated genetic risk and increasingly sedentary Western lifestyles, that message is both a warning and an opportunity.

*The study, led by Dr. Tao Zhang at Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, was published in JAMA Network Open in June 2026.*
